newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Top officials dismissed in U.N. Rwanda tribunal.
newsitem.headline: Top officials dismissed in U.N. Rwanda tribunal.

text.p: Secretary-General Kofi Annan on Wednesday dismissed two top officials of the Rwanda genocide tribunal following a U.N. probe that found widespread mismanagement and financial waste.

The two were the tribunal's deputy prosecutor, Honoure Rakotomanana, a judge from Madagascar, and the registrar, Andonico Adede of Kenya, who in effect served as chief administrator for the court based in Arusha, Tanzania.

"The secretary-general decided that the continuation of two officials of the tribunal in their posts would not be in the interests of the United Nations and of the work of the tribunal in a case involving human tragedy of incalculable proportion," U.N. spokesman Juan-Carlos Brandt said.

Adede was replaced by Agwu Ukiwe Okali of Nigeria, a graduate of the London School of Economics and Harvard Law School, who is currently serving in the U.N. Habitat office in Nairobi. But a new deputy prosecutor has not yet been named, Brandt said.

The tribunal is to try those alleged to be responsible for the slaughter by Hutu troops and militia of more than half a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994. A total of 21 people have been indicted.
A report released two weeks ago by Karl Paschke, the U.N. equivalent of an inspector-general, detailed administrative mismanagement, unqualified staff and legal chaos.
Despite examples of financial abuse throughout the report, Paschke said he found no cases of outright fraud.

He also criticised New York headquarters, including the departments of legal affairs, headed by Hans Corell of Sweden and the administration and management, headed by Joseph Connor of the United States, for not providing proper support.
But Annan on Wednesday did not take any action against anyone in New York.
Brandt said that Corell's deputy, Ralph Zacklin of Britain, who had handled much of the legal work for the tribunal, was appointed acting U.N. human rights commissioner in Geneva.
He replaces temporarily Jose Ayala Lasso, the new foreign minister of Ecuador.

The prosecutor for the tribunal is Louise Arbour of Canada, who is also prosecutor for the Hague-based U.N. tribunal on war crimes in the former Yugoslavia. Arbour, Adede and Rakotomanana came to New York on Friday for meetings with Annan.

In his report, Paschke recommended that the deputy prosecutor, based in Kigali, the Rwandan capital, be replaced. But despite strong criticisms of Adede, he said the Kenyan, who had worked in the New York legal affairs department, faced untold obstacles with few resources to get the court organised.
Nevertheless, diplomats said he left Annan little choice in dismissing Adede. Paschke's report said that "not a single administrative area ... functioned effectively."

The case became the first test for Annan, who took office on Jan. 1 and is under pressure to reform the organisation and reduce waste and inefficiency following a U.S. campaign to deny his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali, a second term.
